title: Complexity Analysis & Big-O
summary: Predict whether your code survives a 1000× bigger input — without running it. Big-O is the senior engineer's first instinct when something is slow at scale.

blocks.markdown:
Big-O measures how an algorithm's *work* grows as the input grows — not how many seconds it takes.

- We count abstract **steps**, because seconds depend on machine, language, and load.
- **Big-O** is an **upper bound**: "does at most this much work for large `n`," up to a constant.
- Throw away constants and lower-order terms: `O(3n + 5)` is just **O(n)**.
- A 10× CPU buys a constant speedup; the wrong complexity class loses by factors that grow without limit.

blocks.subTitle: Read the input limit
blocks.markdown:
The input size in a problem statement often tells you the target complexity before you've solved anything.

| Input limit | Intended complexity |
|---|---|
| n ≤ 10⁶ | O(n) or O(n log n) |
| n ≤ 10⁴ | O(n²) is fine |
| n ≤ 20 | O(2ⁿ) bitmask / backtracking |
| n ≤ 12 | O(n!) permutations |

blocks.subTitle: O, Ω, Θ
blocks.markdown:
Three bounds describe how the operation count behaves for large `n`.

- **Big-O** — upper bound, "grows no faster than." Used most; defaults to worst case.
- **Big-Omega (Ω)** — lower bound, "grows at least as fast as." Comparison sorts are Ω(n log n).
- **Big-Theta (Θ)** — tight, both at once. People say "O" but usually mean Θ.
- **Worst/average/best case** is a *separate axis*: it picks *which input*, not the growth shape.

blocks.subTitle: The two simplification rules
blocks.markdown:
Two rules cover almost every analysis — and they're *why* Big-O transfers across machines.

- **Drop constant factors.** `O(2n)`, `O(100n)`, `O(n/2)` are all **O(n)**.
- **Drop lower-order terms.** `O(n² + n + 1000)` is just **O(n²)** — only the fastest-growing piece survives.
- Everything machine-specific lives in the constants and small terms you just discarded.
- Log base doesn't matter: `log₂n` and `log₁₀n` differ by a constant, so both are **O(log n)**.

blocks.subTitle: The complexity ladder
blocks.markdown:
Feel these in your bones, flattest to steepest. The *class* swamps every other detail at scale.

![Growth-rate curves of common complexity classes](assets/complexity-big-o/growth-rates.svg)

- **O(1)** constant, **O(log n)** one step per doubling, **O(n)** linear, **O(n log n)** linearithmic.
- **O(n²)** every pair interacts; **O(2ⁿ)** doubles per added element; **O(n!)** every ordering.
- O(1) and O(log n) stay nearly flat; O(n²) and up shoot almost straight up.

assets.alt: Growth-rate curves of common complexity classes

blocks.subTitle: Analyzing loops
blocks.markdown:
Nested loops **multiply**; sequential loops **add**, then keep the biggest term.

```python
for x in arr:          # O(n)
    work(x)

for i in arr:          # O(n^2): nested
    for j in arr:
        work(i, j)

for i in range(n):     # O(log n): index doubles
    i *= 2
```

- Read the *bound*, not the variable name: `for j in range(i, n)` still sums to ≈ n²/2.
- An index that multiplies or halves each step runs only **log n** times.

blocks.subTitle: Recursion & the Master Theorem
blocks.markdown:
Analyze recursion with a **recurrence**, then solve it. Merge sort: `T(n) = 2·T(n/2) + n`.

![Recursion tree for T(n)=2T(n/2)+n](assets/complexity-big-o/master-theorem-tree.svg)

- For `T(n) = a·T(n/b) + f(n)`, compare `f(n)` against the leaf cost `n^(log_b a)`; the bigger wins.
- Merge sort: leaf cost `n` *equals* `f(n) = n` → **Θ(n log n)** (Master Theorem case 2).
- Each tree level does the same total work `n`, across `log n` levels → `n log n`.

blocks.subTitle: Amortized analysis
blocks.markdown:
Amortized cost asks: what's the *average* per operation over a long run?

![Amortized cost of dynamic-array doubling](assets/complexity-big-o/amortized-doubling.svg)

- A dynamic array doubles when full — a rare **O(n)** copy among many cheap **O(1)** pushes.
- Copy work across `n` pushes is `1 + 2 + 4 + … + n < 2n`, so per-push cost is a small constant.
- Resizes get exponentially *rarer* as the array grows, diluting their cost → **O(1) amortized**.

blocks.subTitle: Time vs space, asymptotics vs constants
blocks.markdown:
Big-O guides design, but knowing its limits is what makes it useful.

- **Time vs space** — memoization buys speed with memory; a hash set makes "seen this?" O(1) at O(n) memory. All of DP is this trade ([dynamic-programming-1](dynamic-programming-1)).
- **Asymptotics vs constants** — insertion sort (O(n²)) beats quicksort for n under ~10, so real libraries switch for tiny subarrays.
- **Worst vs average** — a hash table is O(1) average, O(n) worst; adversarial input pushes you to worst-case guarantees.

blocks.subTitle: Quick decision rules
blocks.markdown:
Let the input shape pick the target before you design.

- Input can be large (n > 10⁵)? An O(n²) solution will likely time out — aim O(n log n) or better.
- See O(2ⁿ) or O(n!)? Hunt for overlapping subproblems (→ DP) or a greedy shortcut first.
- Reads dominate and memory is cheap? **Precompute and cache** to drop a query O(n) → O(1).
- n guaranteed tiny? Prefer the simplest correct algorithm; don't over-engineer the Big-O.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
Complexity reasoning drives real production design.

- **Postgres planner** weighs an O(n) sequential scan against an O(log n) B-tree index — and picks the scan for tiny tables ([relational-db-internals](relational-db-internals)).
- **Java HashMap** treeifies a long bucket to bound the worst case at O(log n), not O(n) ([hashing](hashing)).
- **Dynamic arrays** double their buffer so append is O(1) amortized ([arrays-strings](arrays-strings)).
- **Spark joins** swap an O(n×m) nested join for a hash/sort-merge join at petabyte scale.

blocks.subTitle: Signals in production
blocks.markdown:
Big-O leaves fingerprints all over production. Watch for:

- **Latency rising with data size** — plot p99 against row count; a straight line screams O(n), a curve screams O(n²).
- **"Worked in staging"** — toy data hid a bad complexity class; test at production scale.
- **N+1 queries** — one DB call per item turns an O(1) page load into O(n) round-trips.
- **`item in list` inside a loop** — silently O(n²), hidden until the list grows.
- **Periodic latency blips** — a rare amortized resize firing ([caching](caching)).

The misconceptions that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Big-O tells me how fast my code runs."** No — it's the *shape* of the curve, not a wall-clock number.
- **"Big-O always means worst case."** It's an upper bound on *whatever case* you analyze; worst case is just convention.
- **"Nested loops are always O(n²)."** Only if both bounds scale with `n`. Read the actual bounds.
- **"Amortized O(1) means every op is O(1)."** It's the *average*; a single resize is still O(n).
- **"Space is just what I allocate."** The recursion call stack counts — depth `n` is O(n) space.
